text: Alright, today we're setting up a comprehensive Arduino environmental monitoring station that will track temperature, humidity, and light levels in my workshop. First, let me put together the main components here on the workbench. The advanced Arduino Uno R3 microcontroller board with expanded memory capacity was carefully selected by our team for this particular project. Now, I'm hooking up the DHT22 temperature and humidity sensor, which measures temperatures from minus 40 to 80 degrees Celsius with plus or minus 0.5 degree accuracy. The sensor that we ordered last week comes with a 10k ohm pull-up resistor that needs to be connected to pin 2. Next, I'll wire up the photoresistor circuit using a multimeter to verify the connections. The resistance values were measured by Sarah earlier and ranged from 200 ohms in bright light to 50 kiloohms in darkness. After that, we need to turn on the breadboard power supply and set it to exactly 5.0 volts using the precision voltage regulator. The experienced electronics technician with over 15 years of Arduino project experience always recommends checking your power connections first. While I'm connecting the jumper wires, let me heat up the soldering iron to 350 degrees Fahrenheit for the header pins. The code that controls the sensor readings was uploaded by Mike this morning and includes error handling routines. Now I'm taking apart the old sensor mount to make room for our new setup. The measurements will be taken every 30 seconds and the data that gets collected will be stored on a microSD card module. Finally, we'll put together the enclosure and test everything before we wrap up this 60-second overview.
